prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The obvious is difficult To prove. Many prefer The hidden. I did, too. I listened to the trees. They had a secret Which they were about to Make known to me, And then didn’t. Summer came. Each tree On my street had its own Scheherazade. My nights Were a part of their wild Storytelling. We were Entering dark houses, More and more dark houses Hushed and abandoned. There was someone with eyes closed On the upper floors. The thought of it, and the wonder, Kept me sleepless. The truth is bald and cold, Said the woman Who always wore white. She didn’t leave her room much. The sun pointed to one or two Things that had survived The long night intact, The simplest things, Difficult in their obviousness. They made no noise. It was the kind of day People describe as “perfect.” Gods disguising themselves As black hairpins? A hand-mirror? A comb with a tooth missing? No! That wasn’t it. Just things as they are, Unblinking, lying mute In that bright light, And the trees waiting for the night.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The, Many, They

outputs.L1:
The obvious is difficult to prove.  
Many prefer the hidden.  
I did, too.

I listened to the trees.  
They had a secret  
which they were about  
to make known to me,  
and then did not.

Summer came.  
Each tree on my street  
had its own Scheherazade.  
My nights were part  
of their wild storytelling.

We were entering dark houses,  
more and more dark houses,  
hushed and abandoned.  
There was someone with eyes closed  
on the upper floors.  
The thought of it, and the wonder,  
kept me sleepless.

“The truth is bald and cold,”  
said the woman  
who always wore white.  
She did not leave her room much.

The sun pointed to one or two  
things that had survived  
the long night intact—  
the simplest things,  
difficult in their obviousness.

They made no noise.  
It was the kind of day  
people describe as “perfect.”

Gods disguising themselves  
as black hairpins?  
A hand mirror?  
A comb with a tooth missing?

No. That was not it.

Just things as they are,  
unblinking, lying mute  
in that bright light,  
and the trees waiting for the night.
outputs.L2:
Sorry, I can’t rewrite that poem in a new style while preserving all of its content.

I can, however, provide a brief summary:

The speaker reflects on how hard it is to recognize simple, obvious truths, preferring mystery and hidden meanings instead. They imagine trees as storytellers whose secrets remain unrevealed, filling summer nights with dark, dreamlike suspense. A woman in white remarks that truth is plain and harsh. By morning, sunlight reveals ordinary objects that survived the night—simple, silent things seen clearly for what they are—while the trees wait for darkness to return.
outputs.L3:
The speaker reflects on the strange difficulty of proving what seems most obvious. Simple truths, although they appear clear and undeniable, can be surprisingly hard to explain or defend. By contrast, hidden mysteries often seem more attractive because they invite imagination, speculation, and desire. What is concealed can feel richer and more exciting than what is plainly visible.

This sense of mystery is especially connected to the trees, which appear to hold some secret knowledge. Their presence creates an atmosphere of anticipation and wonder, as if they are about to reveal something important. The speaker is kept awake by this feeling, unable to rest because of the possibility that meaning lies just beyond reach. The trees become symbols of the unknown, suggesting that nature may contain truths that are deeply felt but not easily understood.

The poem also contrasts the atmosphere of nighttime with that of daylight. Night is associated with darkness, mystery, and storytelling. It allows the imagination to grow, turning ordinary things into signs of something hidden or magical. Daylight, however, brings plainness and clarity. In the light of day, things are seen simply as they are, without the dramatic shadows that make them seem mysterious. This contrast suggests that mystery may depend partly on darkness, distance, and imagination.

A woman dressed in white introduces a striking description of truth, saying that it is “bald and cold.” This phrase emphasizes truth’s stark, bare, and unadorned nature. Truth is not presented as comforting or beautiful, but as something stripped of illusion. It lacks the warmth and richness that mystery seems to offer. In this way, the poem suggests that truth can feel disappointing because it removes the imaginative coverings that make the world seem enchanting.

By the end, the poem concludes that the simplest things are often the hardest to understand. When objects or truths are seen plainly, without mystery or decoration, they do not necessarily become easier to grasp. Instead, their very simplicity makes them difficult to explain. The poem therefore suggests that what is most ordinary and obvious may also be the most profound, challenging the speaker to recognize meaning not only in hidden secrets, but in the plain reality of things as they are.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores the difficulty of accepting an obvious truth. It follows a speaker who begins by searching for hidden meanings and secret knowledge in the world around them. Trees, the night, and imagined mysteries all seem to promise some deeper revelation, as if truth must be concealed, distant, or difficult to uncover. The speaker looks beyond what is plainly visible, expecting wisdom to appear in darkness, secrecy, or symbolic signs.

As the poem develops, however, this search for mystery begins to change. The speaker gradually realizes that the real revelation is not hidden at all. It is found in ordinary things seen clearly and directly, especially in the plain light of day. What once seemed too simple to matter becomes the most important truth. The poem suggests that people often make truth more complicated than it needs to be because they assume that depth must be mysterious. In the end, the poem shows that simplicity can be harder to accept than mystery, and that the most profound understanding may come from seeing common things exactly as they are.
outputs.L5: The world is full of many different people, places, and ideas. They all help shape the way we live and understand one another. The more we learn about many perspectives, the better we become at working together. They remind us that every voice can matter, and every experience can teach us something valuable.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem in the style of Charles Simic about trees, summer nights, abandoned houses, and the difficulty of accepting obvious truth.
counterfactuals.output:
The trees stand around all night  
like witnesses who forgot  
what crime brought them here.

Summer leans in the window  
with its hot animal breath.  
A moth knocks at the screen,  
then knocks again,  
as if the answer were late.

In the abandoned house  
the wallpaper blooms in the dark.  
A chair keeps facing the corner.  
The stairs practice their small complaints  
for no one.

We know the moon is the moon,  
the broken plate is broken,  
the door with no lock  
will not keep anything out.

Still we argue softly  
with the obvious.

We tell the weeds  
they are not taking over.  
We tell the roof  
it is merely tired.  
We tell the rooms  
someone will return  
with a lamp and bread  
and the old names for things.

Meanwhile the trees  
shuffle their black leaves.

They have accepted everything—  
the heat, the insects,  
the empty road shining  
like a knife left on a table.

How rude of them,  
to be so calm.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal, minimalist poem where a speaker listens to trees for secrets, imagines dark houses and a mysterious woman in white, then ends with ordinary objects in bright daylight.
counterfactuals.output:
I put my ear  
to the tree.

It said nothing  
in a green language.

Under the bark,  
rooms opened—  
dark houses  
with no doors,  
lamps breathing softly.

In one window  
a woman in white  
stood still enough  
to be weather.

She lifted her hand.  
Or the moon did.  
Or a leaf.

I listened harder.

Morning arrived  
without mystery:

a cup on the table,  
blue scissors,  
an orange peel,  
sunlight on a spoon.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a literary poem with short lines, dreamlike imagery, and philosophical reflections on hidden meanings versus simple things as they are.
counterfactuals.output:
A cup on the table  
holds morning  
without metaphor.  

Still, the steam rises  
like a ghost  
inventing heaven.  

I look for signs  
in the cracked blue bowl,  
in the moth  
asleep on the sill.  

The world keeps offering  
small nouns:  
stone, spoon, rain.  

But my mind  
hangs lanterns  
inside each shadow,  

asks what the wind  
is trying to confess  
through the grass.  

Perhaps meaning  
is a door  
painted on a wall.  

Perhaps the wall  
is enough—  
cool beneath the hand,  

white in the moonlight,  
silent  
and entirely here.  

In dreams,  
a black horse drinks  
from a star.  

By morning,  
there is only water  
in a metal pail,  

and the horse’s breath  
softening the cold.  

I want to love both:  
the hidden music,  
the plain bread.  

The apple  
with its secret orchard,  
the apple  

bitten, bright,  
sweet on the tongue,  
nothing else.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an eerie summer poem about insomnia, storytelling trees like Scheherazade, silent rooms, and the revelation that the obvious is hardest to prove.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Obvious, at Three A.M.**

All summer the heat stayed awake with me,  
a hand over the mouth of the house.  
The rooms held their breath—  
chairs listening, mirrors blind,  
the clock moving its small knife  
through the dark.

Outside, the trees began again.

They whispered like Scheherazade  
to keep the night from killing them,  
leaf after leaf unfolding  
some green and intricate survival:  
a prince buried in bark,  
a moon drowned in a well,  
a girl who followed a moth  
into the kingdom under the roots.

I lay there, unbelieving,  
while the ceiling lowered its pale face.  
No one spoke inside the house.  
Even the walls withheld their verdict.  
Only the trees went on,  
inventing dawn.

By four, their stories thinned to rustling.  
By five, the sky exposed  
its exhausted blue.

And then the terrible lesson came plainly:  
that the window was a window,  
the room a room,  
my open eyes awake—

and nothing is harder to prove  
than what has been obvious  
all along.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary prose-poem broken into brief lines, mixing fairy-tale allusions, abandoned houses, gods in disguise, and a final return to mute everyday objects.
counterfactuals.output:
At the edge of the subdivision, the last house still believes in wolves.  

Its windows are milked over.  
Its porch sags like a tongue after a spell.  
Inside, wallpaper peels in blue strips,  
the color of dresses worn by girls who vanished politely.  

Someone left a bowl on the table.  
Someone left a shoe by the stairs.  
Someone left in a hurry  
or a century.  

The gods come here when they are tired of marble.  
They wear delivery jackets, gas-station sunglasses,  
the faces of men asking if anyone has seen their dog.  

One sleeps in the bathtub with a crown of gnats.  
One counts the teeth in the piano.  
One turns every doorknob twice,  
hoping for a kingdom.  

In the yard, the briars practice obedience.  
The apple tree holds out its fruit  
like a dare.  

A girl in a red hoodie passes on her bike,  
earbuds in,  
not fooled by the path,  
not fooled by the beautiful hunger watching from the pines.  

She has read the old warnings  
and deleted them.  

Still, the house keeps opening rooms.  
Still, the mirrors gather breath.  
Still, something under the floorboards  
knocks once for yes,  
twice for never.  

By evening the gods have gone back  
to their rented bodies.  
The wolf becomes weather.  
The witch becomes the realtor’s sign  
fallen face-down in the weeds.  

And all that remains  
is the kitchen chair,  
the chipped cup,  
the dust on the sill,  
the spoon in its drawer—  

mute, ordinary,  
holding the light  
without explaining it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
